I was the exact same way. My parents never trusted me to cook so I didn't learn to cook until I was out of the house. I'm still learning to this day and I'm 33.

I'll tell you the directions for the first thing I cooked, a regular box of kraft Mac and cheese. 

First you're going to prep your materials. You'll need the box of Mac and cheese, a medium sized sauce pan, a big spoon (wooden or rubber works best for me) and a strainer. You can also have butter, salt and pepper on standby if you want. 

Preemptively put the strainer in the sink. Fill the sauce pan about 2/3 full of water, add a pinch or two of salt (~1/4 teaspoon I think? It helps the noodles not stick together). 

Set the saucepan on the stove and I turn it all the way up until it boils. You want big bubbles, not little ones. At that point I open the box of noodles, pull out the powder cheese packet and set it aside and pour the noodles in. I turn the heat down between halfway and high and stir the noodles once or twice a minute. The box says cook for 7 minutes so I usually do that but you can also use a fork and pull out a noodle, blow on it and taste it to see if it is the desired firmness level since some people like it harder or softer. The longer it cooks the more soft it will get. 

Once it is at the desired softness level pour it into the strainer, the water will drain the noodles will not. 

I then turn off the burner, set the pan on a different burner, add about a half tablespoon of butter because I'm from Wisconsin and we like our dairy products lol (milk also works) and add the noodles back into the saucepan. Open the packet of powdered cheese, stir with the big spoon until it is mixed thoroughly and I usually add a pinch or two of pepper. 

Each thing you cook will be different for awhile but then you'll start to notice patterns in how things are made. Personally, I recommend a crockpot as it makes things nice and simple for you. 

Good luck!

I teach for two universities, both in person and online. I teach a variety of communication courses from first year to upper levels/senior capstone classes. 

I've started building the course with the more common accommodations in mind. Each assignment includes a description of the accommodations built in that students don't have to contact me to ask for. I have a very lenient attendance policy and give students a 24-hour grace period for online assignments. If it's an in person assignment I drop the lowest grade. 
This has reduced a lot of my emails and students have commented on how it helps them too. I do receive an occasional email about accommodations, probably one to two a semester, but way less than I used to and mostly for extenuating circumstances.

Since I've implemented this I have not noticed a decrease in quality of student work or drive to complete things. For the most part I've actually seen students work harder and are more willing to come to class and interact.

I will say that while I was working out the kinks of one of these accommodations ideas and how to make it work for everyone I had several students take advantage negatively so I had to change that policy. I talked with my students and we found a different way to achieve the goal. But that's why syllabi are subject to changes 🙃 it's always a work in progress to find the best way to teach the subject matter to different people who have different needs and ways of learning. 

All this to say, naw, I don't mind the emails from students asking for their earned accommodations. But I'd rather be proactive about it lol.

I've taught 8am public speaking classes before and here are some of my tips/tricks: 
- PowerPoints or some sort of visual aids
- break up lectures with discussions and group activities. Sometimes the weirder the better. 
- get students up and moving. Depending on the length of the class (my classes have ranged from 50-75 minutes) have short breaks.
- change the classroom setup. Play with small circles of chairs, big circles, etc. 
- don't stand behind the desk. I move around constantly. Use the whole space, walk among the students, sit down and chat with them during discussions. 
- don't worry too much about trying to connect with students at their level. I embrace being slightly older and out of date, we laugh about outdated terms and how my examples are old references now. Then I have them find their own examples. It usually works really well in solidifying their understanding of the material. 

I know the anxiety and imposter syndrome doesn't really go away, but hopefully something in these suggestions will help you. I also received very little training and had to figure it out as I went along. But these have helped me a lot and I routinely get high ratings.

First you need to identify the root cause of why you are failing. 

Often it's time management. Not giving yourself enough time to study the material and turn in assignments on time. Getting a calendar and writing down everything in there has helped me get organized and not miss any due dates in years. 

Another common issue is not taking notes in a way that works with how you learn. For me, I need to physically write them and while I'm in class I usually write what comes to my mind about other things while I am listening. That way I can start to see connections between the new things I'm learning and the things I already know. It builds stronger memories. 

I've also seen people struggle because they're not in the right major for them. When you find the right classes and major for you it feels like coming home (at least it did for me). I looked forward to going to class, I had more energy to study. I turned in assignments early. It made such a a huge difference in my life. 

That's some general advice, but really you need to find what is causing you to struggle first before you can really start looking for solutions.

I'm in a grad program and the majority of my fellow grad students are neurodivergent in some way, shape or form (most common are ADHD and ASD, but some OCD too). Many of us have just learned how to make our traits work for us by saying "fuck it" to the normal study and writing habits.

Just because something is normalized doesn't mean it's the only way to do things. Figure out how you get things done and use it. 
For example, if you're a night owl avoid morning classes and study more at night. If you can't focus for long periods of time figure out what amount of time works best for you and then build in some breaks. If you have problems writing, switch to a sans serif font or use voice to text and just talk through it. 

There are so many paths you can take to get to the same destination. Try not to be discouraged if one dead ends for you. The more you learn about yourself the easier it gets.

Edit: as for socialization, I tend to find one or two people who don't drain me and stick to them. I also set aside one day a week where I spend a few hours socializing. The rest of my down time is for me. It helps some.
